meta.titre: Waves: properties, wave types and the wave equation
meta.sous_theme: wave properties and the electromagnetic spectrum

sections.contenu_markdown: A fisherman on Lake Barombi watches a floating cork bob up and down as ripples spread across the water, yet the cork does not travel to the shore with the ripples. In the same way, the sound of a drum at a village festival and the radio signal that carries the news to your house both spread out from their source without any material moving with them. A wave is a way of carrying energy, and the GCE asks you to name its properties, to distinguish the two types of wave and to use $v=f\lambda$.

items: Speed is the distance travelled divided by the time taken.
A vibration is a repeated back-and-forth movement, and one complete vibration is one cycle.
Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), where $1\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is one cycle per second.

sections.titre: Properties of waves, the two types of wave and the wave equation
sections.contenu_markdown:
A **wave** transfers **energy** from one place to another without transferring matter. The particles of the medium vibrate about fixed positions.

**Wave quantities.**

| Quantity | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| Amplitude $a$ | maximum displacement from the rest (mean) position | m |
| Wavelength $\lambda$ | distance between two successive crests (or two identical points) | m |
| Frequency $f$ | number of complete waves passing a point per second | Hz |
| Period $T$ | time for one complete wave, $T=\dfrac{1}{f}$ | s |
| Wave speed $v$ | distance travelled by a crest per second | $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ |

**The wave equation:**

$$v=f\lambda$$

**Two types of wave.**

| | Transverse | Longitudinal |
|---|---|---|
| Vibration | at right angles to the direction of travel | along (parallel to) the direction of travel |
| Pattern | crests and troughs | compressions and rarefactions |
| Examples | light and all electromagnetic waves, water ripples, waves on a rope | sound waves |

**Reading a wave:** the *amplitude* of a sound wave controls its **loudness**; its *frequency* controls its **pitch**. A mechanical wave (water, sound) needs a medium to travel in, but electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum.

**Resonance.** When a system is made to vibrate at its **natural frequency** by an external vibration of the same frequency, its amplitude becomes very large. Examples: pushing a swing at the right moment, a glass breaking at a certain note, tuning a radio to a station.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to order, compare or give uses of radio waves, light, X-rays and similar waves.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
In order of **increasing frequency** (decreasing wavelength): radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light (red to violet), ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.

All of them are transverse, carry energy, travel through a vacuum and travel at the **same speed in a vacuum**, $c=3.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. They differ in frequency and wavelength, so $c=f\lambda$ holds for each.

Uses: radio waves for broadcasting, microwaves for mobile phones and cooking, infrared for remote controls, visible light for sight, ultraviolet for sterilising, X-rays for medical images, gamma rays for treating cancer and sterilising equipment.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question concerns speed of sound, echoes, pitch or loudness.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Sound is a longitudinal wave and needs a medium: it cannot travel through a vacuum. In air its speed is about $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; it is faster in liquids and fastest in solids because the particles are closer together. Humans hear frequencies from about $20\ \mathrm{Hz}$ to $20\,000\ \mathrm{Hz}$. For example, a tuning fork of frequency $440\ \mathrm{Hz}$ in air has a wavelength $\lambda=\dfrac{330}{440}=0.75\ \mathrm{m}$. Distance to an object $=\dfrac{v\times t}{2}$ when the sound goes to the object and back.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A cork floats on a pond. Water waves pass it and the cork bobs up and down $20$ times in $40\ \mathrm{s}$. The distance between successive crests is $1.5\ \mathrm{m}$.

(a) Find the frequency and the period of the waves.

(b) Find the speed of the waves.

(c) How long does a crest take to travel $30\ \mathrm{m}$ across the pond?

etapes.justification: Frequency is the number of waves per second.
The period is the reciprocal of the frequency, $T=1/f$.
The wavelength is the distance between successive crests.
Time is distance divided by speed.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **(a)** $f=0.50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $T=2.0\ \mathrm{s}$. **(b)** $v=0.75\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. **(c)** $t=40\ \mathrm{s}$. The cork only bobs up and down: the wave carries energy, not water, to the shore.

items.erreur_markdown: “A wave carries the water (or the air) from the source to the receiver.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Particles of the medium only vibrate about their rest positions. What travels is energy.
items.correction_markdown: A wave transfers energy without transferring matter.

items.erreur_markdown: “A louder sound has a higher frequency.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Frequency determines the pitch. Loudness depends on the amplitude of the vibration.
items.correction_markdown: Louder sound: larger amplitude. Higher pitch: higher frequency.

items.erreur_markdown: “X-rays travel faster than radio waves in a vacuum because they have more energy.”
items.pourquoi_faux: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum. X-rays have a higher frequency and a shorter wavelength.
items.correction_markdown: In a vacuum all electromagnetic waves have speed $c=3.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

items.erreur_markdown: Measuring the amplitude from the bottom of a trough to the top of a crest.
items.pourquoi_faux: That distance is twice the amplitude. Amplitude is measured from the rest (mean) position.
items.correction_markdown: Amplitude = maximum displacement from the rest position, i.e. half the crest-to-trough height.

items.erreur_markdown: “Sound can travel through a vacuum but light cannot.”
items.pourquoi_faux: It is the other way round. Sound is a mechanical wave and needs particles; light is an electromagnetic wave and can cross a vacuum.
items.correction_markdown: Sound needs a medium; light does not.

items.enonce_markdown: An AM radio station broadcasts at a frequency of $6.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Radio waves travel at $3.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in air. Calculate the wavelength of the waves.

During a storm, a child sees a flash of lightning and hears the thunder $6.0\ \mathrm{s}$ later. Take the speed of sound in air as $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and treat the light as arriving instantly.

(a) Calculate the distance between the child and the lightning.

(b) State why sound cannot arrive instantly.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Distance $=$ speed $\times$ time $=330\times6.0=$ **$1980\ \mathrm{m}$** (about $2\ \mathrm{km}$).

(b) Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave which passes from particle to particle, so it travels at only about $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in air, whereas light travels at $3.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

items.enonce_markdown:
A wave on a long rope has amplitude $0.050\ \mathrm{m}$ and wavelength $0.40\ \mathrm{m}$. Five complete waves pass a fixed point in $2.0\ \mathrm{s}$.

(a) Calculate the frequency and period of the wave.

(b) Calculate the speed of the wave.

(c) The hand is moved faster so that the frequency doubles, but the rope and its tension stay the same, so the speed is unchanged. Calculate the new wavelength.

(d) State whether the wave on the rope is transverse or longitudinal if the hand moves up and down at right angles to the rope.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $f=\dfrac{5}{2.0}=$ **$2.5\ \mathrm{Hz}$**, and $T=\dfrac{1}{2.5}=$ **$0.40\ \mathrm{s}$**.

(b) $v=f\lambda=2.5\times0.40=$ **$1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$**.

(c) The new frequency is $5.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and the speed is still $1.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so $\lambda=\dfrac{v}{f}=\dfrac{1.0}{5.0}=$ **$0.20\ \mathrm{m}$**.

(d) **Transverse**, because the vibration is at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels along the rope.

items_markdown: A wave transfers energy without transferring matter; the amplitude is measured from the rest position.
Wave equation: $v=f\lambda$; period $T=\dfrac{1}{f}$; frequency is in hertz and wavelength in metres.
Transverse waves (light, water, rope) vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel; longitudinal waves (sound) vibrate along it.
Loudness depends on amplitude, pitch on frequency; sound needs a medium and cannot travel in a vacuum.
All electromagnetic waves travel at $3.0\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in a vacuum and differ in frequency and wavelength.
Resonance is a large-amplitude vibration produced when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency.
